extracted.intended_audience: IP attorneys, in-house counsel, patent litigators, and stakeholders in standard-essential patents (SEPs) and FRAND licensing
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes legal standards and evidentiary considerations that courts have applied in litigation and administrative proceedings concerning standard-essential patents (SEPs) and commitments to license on fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory (FRAND) terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparable licenses as market-based evidence of SEP value
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge Gilstrap found that the comparable licenses presented by Ericsson to be “the best market-based evidence” of the value of Ericsson’s standard essential patents (SEPs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court preference for showing value through existing market transactions: present comparable licenses as primary evidence of SEP value rather than novel litigation constructs. Use real-world license terms when possible to support royalty calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of SSPPU methodology absent market evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The market evidence, in the form of comparable licenses, has failed to embrace HTC’s preferred SSPPU [smallest salable patent-practicing unit] methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on SSPPU (e.g., basing royalties on a baseband chip cost) unless there is concrete evidence that industry licenses are negotiated on that basis. Courts may reject SSPPU if industry practice doesn't support that apportionment; show why SSPPU reflects actual market negotiation if asserting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEP value can exceed component (chip) value — apportionment must reflect market reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence showed that the value of SEPs can exceed the value of the chip, which price does not include the cost of that intellectual property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When performing apportionment or arguing appropriate royalty base, account for the possibility that SEPs contribute value beyond the price of a single component; provide evidence tying patent value to device-level value where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-based evidence preferred over litigation-based top-down analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: This SEP cases is one of the closest to capturing what actually happens in the licensing market with FRAND-committed SEPS, rather than generating new litigation-based theories on valuing SEPs (e.g., top-down analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may view top-down or novel litigation-devised valuation approaches skeptically; favor evidence reflecting actual licensing practice and market comparables.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRAND status may affect royalty outcomes — analyze relative technology value
rubrics_metrics.description: A jury awarded a much higher royalty for a non-FRAND patent compared to combined royalties for several FRAND-committed SEPs; it was unclear whether the difference was due to the FRAND commitment or relative value of technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing damages and reasonable royalties, consider both FRAND commitments and the intrinsic technical/value differences among patents; be cautious attributing royalty differences solely to FRAND status without evidence of relative technology contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional limits: courts may confine FRAND determinations to domestic patents and law
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to trial, the court limited the case to determination of FRAND commitments on U.S. patents as a matter of U.S. law and not opining on FRAND commitments for foreign patents under foreign law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect courts to avoid ruling on foreign-law FRAND issues or foreign patents unless those matters are squarely presented; litigants seeking global FRAND determinations may face jurisdictional and choice-of-law hurdles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied waiver can apply for failure to disclose related foreign patent application to SDO
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit ruled that implied waiver may apply where the prior owner of a U.S. patent had a duty to disclose a related foreign patent application to ETSI even though ETSI had rejected that prior patent owner’s proposed contribution to the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A duty-to-disclose failure to an SDO can trigger equitable defenses like implied waiver; analyze chain-of-title and prior owner's disclosure obligations when asserting or defending SEPs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied waiver may not require a showing of reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Among other things, the decision indicates that there may not be a requirement to show reliance on the implied waiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments invoking implied waiver should consider that courts may not demand proof that the SDO or others relied on the nondisclosure; focus on the existence of a duty and the context of nondisclosure in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of interpreting the specific SSO/ETSI IPR Policy with evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision provides insight into the importance of looking to the specific standard setting body’s IPR Policy at issue and providing evidence for interpreting that policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making or defending FRAND/SSO-related claims, ground arguments in the precise language of the applicable IPR policy and marshal record evidence (testimony, contemporaneous documents) to support an interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish disclosure of patents that 'may be' essential vs FRAND commitment when patent 'actually is' essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision highlighted the difference between disclosing patents that 'may be' essential to the standard and a FRAND commitment that arises because the patent 'actually is' essential to the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise in disclosure and pleading: disclose patents that may be essential, and be prepared to show actual essentiality to trigger FRAND obligations; the legal consequences differ depending on the patent's asserted essentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to disclose is not an automatic 'gotcha' — must show unfair advantage from misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to disclose is not a 'gotcha' defense; rather, you must show that the patent owner obtained some unfair advantage by its misconduct in not disclosing the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants alleging nondisclosure should demonstrate how the patent owner's failure to disclose conferred an unfair advantage (e.g., altered negotiations or outcomes), not merely point to nondisclosure alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisions are highly case-specific and depend on the evidentiary record
rubrics_metrics.description: As with many decisions, this case is fairly case-specific as far as interpretation of the ETSI IPR Policy... the Federal Circuit indicated that its decision was based on the specific record evidence–and lack of evidence–before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize holdings beyond the factual record at issue; assemble a thorough evidentiary record to support policy-interpretation or equitable-defense arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent misuse / competition-law claims against SEP owners require showing more than traditional enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition law claims asserted against SEPs may not prevail when patent owners have followed traditional patent enforcement and licensing strategies or even if they breach a FRAND commitment. Rather, there must be something more egregious or deceptive with the particular patent owner’s conduct to give rise to competition law claims required to address harm to competition beyond harm addressed by patent or contract remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To assert antitrust or patent-misuse claims tied to SEP conduct, plead and prove conduct that causes competitive harm beyond ordinary patent enforcement or contractual FRAND breaches (e.g., deception, coercion producing market-wide harm). Examples the court considered (and rejected) included alleged requirements to take worldwide licenses, using threats of foreign injunctions to coerce licensing, disparate licensing terms, and nondisclosure of pool royalties — but these alone may not suffice without additional evidence of competitive harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural expectation: challengers should first seek a license or follow SSO procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: No FRAND breach where respondents failed to first seek a license or follow SSO procedure if license not granted (InterDigital).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties asserting FRAND-related defenses or counterclaims should typically pursue available SSO procedures or first seek a license as required by the relevant process; failing to follow such procedures may weaken FRAND-based arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: EU antitrust 'safe harbour' for willing licensees — implications for injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: European antitrust decisions establish 'safe harbour' for willing licensees of FRAND-encumbered SEPs to avoid an injunction and address the circumstances under which an SEP holder may seek injunctive relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Europe, a party that is a willing licensee (i.e., prepared to take a license on FRAND terms) may be protected from injunctions; analyze jurisdictional antitrust guidance when seeking or resisting injunctive relief for SEPs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative bodies (e.g., ITC) may review claim construction and SEP issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) determined to review in part an ALJ’s decision concerning claim construction and standard essential patent (SEP) issues (337-TA-613).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect administrative tribunals to engage with SEP and claim-construction questions; strategy and evidence for SEPs should account for both district court and administrative processes and potential interlocutory or remand review.
